title: Dealing with existential suffering and palliative sedation in specialized palliative care units in Baden-Württemberg
summary:
Background
In recent years, the practice of palliative sedation—the use of medications to reduce or diminish consciousness at the end of life in people who are suffering intensely and whose suffering cannot be alleviated by other means—has evolved. At the same time, there is ongoing debate about when and how such medications can be used appropriately.
A particular reason for using these medications is existential suffering at the end of life—the profound sense of having lost one’s connection to one’s own values, goals, and identity. Those affected often report feelings of hopelessness, helplessness, fear, a loss of meaning, and a sense of lacking dignity. 
Although current guidelines explicitly cite this form of suffering at the end of life as a possible indication for the use of medications that reduce consciousness, many ethical and practical questions remain unresolved.

Research Question
The aim is to understand how various professionals in palliative care units in Baden-Württemberg experience dealing with existential suffering at the end of life—both in general and with regard to the targeted use of medications that reduce consciousness.

Methodology – Approach
Type of study: Qualitative interviews (face-to-face interviews)
Participants: 30 to 40 professionals from various occupational groups—such as physicians, nurses, social workers, art therapists, music therapists, occupational therapists, physical therapists, and spiritual counselors —who work in specialized palliative care units in Baden-Württemberg
Selection: The aim is to obtain as broad a picture as possible by including individuals of different ages, genders, and levels of professional experience, as well as those with varying attitudes toward medications that reduce consciousness.
Interview procedure: An open-ended guide structures the conversation. Topics include the perception of existential suffering, its recognition within the team, and the decision-making and implementation processes for the use of consciousness-altering medications. The interviews last approximately 60 minutes and are recorded with prior consent.
Analysis: The recordings are transcribed in full. This is followed by a content analysis to identify recurring patterns and central themes.

interventions.name: Non-interventional study involving a single 60- to 90-minute interview using a semi-structured interview guide: From the perspective of palliative care teams, the qualitative interview study aims to explore the extent to which existential suffering is identified and treated in specialized palliative

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
This call for potential participants is directed at all members of inpatient palliative care teams (specialized inpatient settings) in Baden-Württemberg from the nursing, medical, psychosocial, medical-therapeutic, and spiritual professions who have experience with existential suffering and palliative sedation.
Exclusion criteria:
Members of these teams are excluded if they have no experience with existential suffering and/or palliative sedation.
